<P0043> Richard, tell me, has there been a time you failed at something or didn't accomplish something you wanted?
<P0108> Uh, yeah.
<P0108> I'd say in the music business, I have accomplished a lot, but I never really got that hit record.
<P0043> Really? How many records have you made?
<P0108> So, I mean, that's a tough thing to do. Some people are fortunate that way. Well, I got about, I guess I've got about six albums out now.
<P0043> That's pretty good.
<P0108> Yeah, I mean, I got a lot of, people know who we are.
<P0043> That's an accomplishment in itself.
<P0108> I mean, in Europe, I know a lot, you know, I'll walk down the street and people know who I am. Here, they can't get arrested in America.
<P0043> Oh yeah, they know you over there.
<P0043> So what would be the best solution to try to make it, or are you gonna keep trying?
<P0108> Just keep trying. That's what I'm doing now. I've gotten a lot older now, and my band is just kind of hanging loose. I got this deal with the Megatracks thing, so I'm going to work with my daughter, which she's always wanted me to do and always tried to get me to do back when I had my own recording studio that I lost. But so we're working together now. I still got my own recording equipment at home, so I record all the parts and do the songs there, and then I send them to her, and she writes all the lyrics and the melodies, and so we're doing that.
<P0043> Oh, that's cool. Good for you. That's good. And the band's still playing?
<P0108> Yeah.
<P0108> No, the band's not playing.
<P0043> You have stuff on tracks already?
<P0108> Oh, yeah. I already did 10 things with her. Son, and I'm still going. I was working on something last night.
<P0043> That's good.
<P0043> Keep pushing through.
<P0108> Oh, yeah. That's all you can do. It's too late to, you know, be a rocket scientist.
<P0043> You never know. Yep.
<P0108> Was there something that you wanted to achieve that you didn't quite get to do?
<P0043> Hmm.
<P0043> I should have went further with, I did interior design for 16 years.
<P0108> Oh, wow. That's good money in that. Hmm. Wow.
<P0043> Yeah.
<P0043> Yeah, it was great. I started late 80s, 90s. Did it for 16 years. Probably should have stayed with it. We had a lot of good clients. A lot of celebrities. Yeah. Should have stayed with it to see how much further I could go. It just didn't, it didn't, it was getting a little burned out and then the last couple of years were hard and decided to move on.
<P0108> Yeah, that's the thing about it. I did the same thing with the music for me. You know, you get to a certain point, and you just get hit in the head so many times that you just said, you can't give up. That's the thing.
<P0043> You get this plateau. You get a plateau of it's not going. And then after about two years of that, I was like, you know what? I'm going to move on to something else.
<P0108> Yeah.
<P0108> Yeah.
<P0108> Yeah. I thought I would be a rock star by now, but it's like, wrong answer. Okay. Okay.

I lived one week at one parent's and one week at another. So the home life was just too crazy. And I just didn't believe in taking that home with me. But yeah, I think that I would have taken things more seriously. Interesting. Yeah.
<P1298> All right.
<P1298> Interesting. Awesome.

<P1298> Oh, Boston is not walkable. Like it is, but the transit system is so bad and I absolutely hate it. Like I want to fix it.

The other thing to focus on is the I mean, this was like the first city in the country, period. Like everything used to be dirt roads and horses. So we were kind of stuck with this infrastructure that we then had to find a way into. So it's actually impressive, but it sucks.
<P1298> So it's actually Yes. I know that they've kind of fixed the red line. I just think they should put more public transit. Why don't they just add another line? And then there could be less cars on the road, right? Am I crazy?
<P1297> Yeah.
<P1297> Yeah, yep
<P1297> No, I mean but Yes, you are crazy cuz no line What it takes my father was actually part of the big dig which brought the whole highway up below and was part of the Rose Kennedy Greenway thing and before that I People don't realize what it takes to create a line underground. It's billions and billions of dollars. So it's almost like we just have to improve the system that we currently have. But I also think that part of cities building their transportation is a little bit on hold because of the technological advances that all of a sudden we're gonna see simpler trains, simpler ways of electric, all of it. It's like the Acela, like we've slowly started to learn how to really utilize these things. So I'm hoping that a lot of the reluctancy is more about like, well, let's see where this is going. But, I mean, even like, like you take, I know this isn't trans, it's not the T or anything, but you take like self-driving cars or whatever, but you just take that technology. And I feel like lights should be based on that, where... We're all on GPS and all that. So it should more or less be able to measure who is approaching what. I mean, essentially in the future, we could just have a grid that the cars get through the grid itself without a light. So I think that all these things could end up just sort of sorting themselves out in the near future. But that's like 10, 15 years.
<P1298> Yeah.

I was that generation of like... You just got home and your parents weren't home so you just unlocked the door and it was the birth of computers and that stuff. So I think that that, I lived a very, my time frame for things really changing in society was kind of spot on when it comes to technology building and building. I think like middle school landline type stuff with like school dances, I see like my nephew, I see like the kids growing up now and I don't feel like they really have that organic type of like school setting and personal touches and like not having, honestly I think cell phones are terrible these days and I think that it really caused people to isolate, self-isolate

[Dialogue between P1297 and P1299 on 2023-06-26]
<P1297> A successor challenge that I've had in my life, when I was 22, my buddy was getting married in California and I was broke. There was no way I was going to make it, but I was like part of the wedding party. And he told me, he was like, why don't you just come here? They had had three kids. He said, why don't you come here? He lived in Carmel, California. He said, We're freshly married, so we could use somebody to just watch the kids.
<P1299> Thank you. Thank you.
<P1297> So I literally did the guitar and duffel bag, just put my stuff in storage and moved out there. And I was there for six months. And this girl I went to high school with needed a roommate in LA. And it was like the perfect time to sort of get out of their hair. So I moved, but I got down there and realized I didn't have a bed, I didn't have a car. And LA is not a city to not have a car in. I mean, the public transportation is dangerous in spots, it's not frequently used. I remember having a bus transfer in Compton and I had a Palm Pilot in a suit and just literally everybody was looking at me being like, dude, this is not... And the bus driver told me, he was like, never get on this bus again, this is not your bus. Find another way around. Took me forever. I was like a wine salesman. It was an hour and a half bus commute there and back. And that made me become a broker in another company. And I started to raise money as a broker and it built my experience there. And then I ended up getting in television through that. So it was all these like little hurdles that I just sort of blindly went into. And it overall really changed my life in a lot of different ways. All those certain experiences were pretty pivotal.
<P1299> Thank you.
<P1299> That is amazing that you went out thinking one thing and then it turned into another.
<P1297> So I just didn't know what I was going to do. I miss it.
<P1299> That's what's great about being in your 20s. You can just do whatever you want.
<P1297> Yes. Right.
<P1297> And I feel like at some point, I've been telling my little brother's 25, and at some point I'm like, just go somewhere. Go do something that you don't know what you're gonna do. Get out of New England. There's a whole nother country that's crazy. And you grow a lot. You grow a lot from being somewhere else. Especially, I have a big family. They're a little bit smothering. So I think that getting away from my family helped my personal growth. by a lot, I think that if I had stayed here, I would have been the same person that I was before I left.
<P1299> Do it.
<P1299> Yeah. You do.
<P1299> That's amazing. Okay.

[Dialogue between P1297 and P1299 on 2023-05-15]
<P1299> So something that I've always wanted to achieve but haven't had a chance yet is actually, it's something I'm in the middle of achieving. So hopefully I will achieve it completely. So I collect sea glass to the point of obsession. And so what I did about a year ago is I turned it into a little side hustle. And I make all sorts of art out of sea glass. And I sell it, craft fairs and things like that. And I also have it in different gift shops. And so what I would... like to do and do to the various positive kinds of podcasts that I listen to is I think I could really turn this into something like big and maybe leave my real job Because it's just starting out small and it's starting to domino. And so that would be what I would like to achieve, that I would like to leave my regular nine-to-five job and then just do this art full-time. I have a couple of questions. Okay. When it comes to the cardboard, how do you do it? How do you do it?
<P1297> Now,
<P1297> I have a couple questions. One, when it comes to crafts about the sea glass, what do you mean? I've seen lamps filled with sea glass.
<P1299> Oh, yeah. So I have kind of like my own little thing. I make these little frames and then in the frame is like a cute little, say it's two pieces of sea glass, but they look like little birds and they're saying cute little sayings to each other like you are amazing and I have flowers and all these things.
<P1297> So how do you get the sea glass to be in the shape of the bird? Do you just glue them on?
<P1299> Oh no, you just glue it on. Yeah, and then you draw around it and I make key chains and I make ornaments and those are like my main things.
<P1297> OK.
<P1297> Two part question. One, what's your favorite color sea glass? And two, what's the most rare?
<P1299> Okay.
<P1299> So the most rare, I believe, is either orange or red, because I have a chart that says, okay, white's like the most common, well, brown is really common, and then white, and then green, and then, so blue is kind of rare, but I actually own one piece of orange, and I think one red. I think there's also some other rare ones. I should know these by heart. There's yellow, I don't own. So it's good and it's bad. Because some people, when they make art, they can just buy their materials and make whatever they make. But I have to actually find my stuff. So I have three beaches that I go to. They're very secretive. I don't tell anyone where they are or a few people. So not only do I enjoy finding the stuff, because then I know I can use it to make stuff, but it's so much fun to find it.
<P1297> Blue's pretty rare too.
<P1297> Yeah, I don't think I've ever seen that.
<P1297> Right.
<P1297> Yeah.
<P1297> Nova Scotia.
<P1299> And I heard Nova Scotia is a good place.
<P1297> I just went on a... I just went up to Nova Scotia for three weeks on a family thing, and man, sea glass gold.
<P1299> Three weeks?
<P1299> Oh, I got to get there then. Oh, my gosh. Okay.
<P1297> Yeah, we got quite a bit of it. All right, awesome.

[Dialogue between P1297 and P1299 on 2023-05-22]
<P1299> So I'm gonna ask you, what you truly want in life, and what is your deepest and most profound dreams for that?
<P1297> I mean, on a vague level, it's happiness, obviously. And unfortunately, success was never an ambition of mine. And I think as I get older, it obviously has become more important. Like, I want to write direct act. I want to be involved in films. And it takes a lot of discipline, especially for writing. I'm a very good writer, but I'm also very scatterbrained. So I can get an idea. I just can't do the sit down, focus one. I can't see projects through. And I need to find a way to do it, because I know I can. I think a lot of it is environment. my environment's kind of been all over the place a bit. So yeah, I think, and between those, I think that writing, I really wanted, there's a couple really golden scripts that I need to work on that are really wonderful. I think it would be, I think it would sell easily. I just need to kind of harness that.
<P1299> Is it?
<P1299> Is it? Is it?
<P1299> You think you have procrastination?
<P1297> Yeah, I procrastination, I'm a night person. And so it takes, which is fine for a writer, but it's, yeah, I think routine is kind of the key to really doing it. And Stephen King says, you know, just write. It doesn't matter if it's garbage, but first thing he does when he wakes up is writes for an hour. It doesn't matter. what it is, and I think that that's, Hemingway also had a similar thing where it was like, don't write for other people, write for yourself, and then all of a sudden you'll start to find your way through things.
<P1299> Just do it.
<P1299> Wow.
<P1299> Well, I think that's great that you have a goal and that you obviously have talent and know that you're good at it. It sounds like you just have to just do it. Well, I just heard a podcast on the way here that said they do studies on procrastination. And the first thing you have to say to yourself is you have to apologize to yourself. And it sounds weird. You just have to apologize to yourself that you've been procrastinating. And then once you do that, you can get past it and then get closer to doing it.
<P1297> I just need to do it.
<P1297> Yeah, I think that that's self-discovery. That's definitely a big part of it is being a little easier on yourself, I think.
<P1299> Maybe you could try that.
<P1299> That's a great, great goal.

[Dialogue between P1297 and P1299 on 2023-06-05]
<P1299> regret is I was very fortunate to have parents that paid for my four-year degree in college. And I was a good student, whatever. But when it was getting towards the end of the degree, my father offered to have me go for my master's. Now, my degree was in marketing, so kind of like general business. I had no interest in getting my master's at that time. I was like 21. I just wanted to get out, get a job, whatever. And so now I look back like, What was my problem? I could have got like a paid for master's degree, probably in like business administration. What I ended up going on to do didn't require a master's. I was a recruiter for 25 years, like a headhunter recruiter, which really anyone can. I mean, you don't need a degree to do it, but college is just a good overall thing to have. So, I mean, I guess, so I didn't really hurt, I can't really apologize to my parents and say I'm sorry for hurting you, because I don't think that was really, if anything, they probably didn't have to spend more money. But who knows? My life probably would have ended. The path would have been different because I would have had a master's and maybe went down a different path. But I do look back on it and kind of regret it because I just think you can never have enough education, and education certainly doesn't hurt anybody, and it's only a good thing. But I think when you're young, you're young and you're stupid, and you just make silly mistakes. I think it is stupid.
<P1297> Thank you.
<P1297> Yeah.
<P1297> The thing is, though, I mean, the amount of people that use their degrees is so minuscule at this point. It's like, I mean, both my older brothers, I didn't go to college. And a lot of it had to do with, it's so stupid at 18 to be able to think about what you want to do with the rest of your life. it's just seems ridiculous to me that we put that it should be more of a 25 year old type of decision. I mean, when you've like my brother, one had an art degree and it's like from mass art and it's like, what, you know, you don't really use that. He now works for Microsoft. My other brother had an English literature major and just never used it. I think it's more about, and I guess a master's degree, it's more about the master's degree. It's more, yes, definitely. But I don't, I mean, I feel like the school system has to change when it comes to that type of thing, that decision-making process at that age is just not reasonable. Some people need their math class.
<P1299> Thank you.
<P1299> Right.
<P1299> It looks good on the resume.
<P1299> And some people need their master's. Like if you want to be a social worker, like you actually need your master's. If you want to be a nurse practitioner, you need your master's. So some careers require it. So I guess at that point in time, I just didn't see the need for it. But now looking back, again, I just think I'm a proponent of education and I just kind of regret that I didn't take him up on his offer.
<P1297> Right.
<P1297> I'm a huge proponent.
<P1297> Yes. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I can see that. Yeah. I never had that. In fact, I was the younger of three brothers. So by the time my father had wasted all that money on the first two brothers, I was sort of a wild card anyway. So it was like, yeah, maybe you hold off.
<P1299> Yeah.
<P1299> Maybe you should go to college.
<P1297> And here I am.
<P1299> Here you are. Okay.

[Dialogue between P1297 and P1299 on 2023-07-17]
<P1297> Here's a good question. Would you rather be able to speak all foreign languages or be able to speak to animals?
<P1299> So I would definitely choose to speak to the animals.
<P1297> Why?
<P1299> Well, because you know when you come home at the end of the day, your dog is always just so happy to see you. They're just happy. if we could be more like that and, you know, a little more simple. Although, I mean, I think learning all foreign languages would be really cool, but then what would you really do with that?
